Se dice: <em>«efe de equis es aproximada:
Read aloud: “f of x is approximately f of a, plus f prime of a times x minus a”.

The symbol $\approx$ is “approximately equal”: two wavy lines instead of two straight ones.

What it says is simple: to know what $f$ is worth near $a$, start from what it is worth at $a$ and add the gradient times how far you have moved. It is exactly what you do when you say “I am doing 90 an hour, so in two hours I will have covered 180 km”: you replace the real motion by one at constant speed.
Se dice: <em>«efe de equis es igual a pe:
Read aloud: “f of x equals P sub n of x, plus f of order n plus one at c, over n plus one factorial, times x minus a raised to n plus one”.

The important thing is that this is an exact equality, not an approximation: the remainder collects everything the polynomial leaves out.

That mysterious $c$ is a particular point lying between $a$ and $x$. Nobody knows which one — and it does not matter, because to bound the error it is enough to know how large $f^{(n+1)}$ can get on that stretch.
Se dice: <em>«pe de a igual a efe de a,:
Read aloud: “P of a equals f of a, P prime of a equals f prime of a, P second of a equals f second of a…”.

The notation $f^{(n)}$, with the number in brackets on top, is “the $n$-th derivative”: differentiating $n$ times in a row. The brackets are used so it is not confused with a power: $f^{(3)}$ is the third derivative, whereas $f^3$ would be $f$ cubed. For the first few the prime marks $f'$ and $f''$ are still used, because three primes start to be hard to see.
Se dice: <em>«pe sub ene de equis es igu:
Read aloud: “P sub n of x equals f of a, plus f prime of a times x minus a, plus f second of a over two factorial times x minus a squared, and so on”.

The $n!$ in the denominator is the factorial: $3! = 3\cdot2\cdot1 = 6$. It appears because differentiating a power $(x-a)^n$ $n$ times gives precisely that number, and you have to divide to cancel it.

In one sentence: each new term adds one more piece of information about how the function curves. The first gives the height, the second the slant, the third the curvature, the fourth how the curvature changes…
